## F01-continued — 2026-08-19: the numbers reconcile, and the ballot stops counting half of itself

F01 shipped its build work and did not close. Its report did not reconcile, and
the author's phone walkthrough of 2026-08-19 found seven further reader-facing
defects. This session is items 1 through 11 of that brief, in the order given.
**Item 12 is the first item not started.**

### What the reconciliations found, and it was not what anyone expected

**Item 1 — D50's missing 23 were never missing.** F01 reported 902 portraits,
531 mapped to a division and 348 mapping to nothing, and 531 + 348 = 879. The
gap is one CATEGORY, not one number: `photo-review.mts` builds its reach map
from division mappings FIRST and then adds curated-body-roster keys that are not
already present. Those 23 roster-only portraits are reachable, and F01 reported
the division half against the whole. The doc's own committed figure was already
554. The standing figure is now a PARTITION written by the generator, so it
cannot be reported with a component missing:

| | Count |
|---|---|
| **Collected** | **902** |
| reachable via a division mapping | 531 |
| reachable via a curated body roster | 23 |
| reachable by nobody | 348 |

**The 591 → 531 movement is not a movement.** They are two different measures,
and neither is a correction of the other: 591 is the SLOT side — people the
product renders, 591 of 751 with a portrait — and it is unchanged today. 531 is
one component of the MANIFEST side. The old-method number for 2026-08-19 is 591.
The denominator moved 750 → 751 because F01 added Dr. Gabriel Trujillo to the
TUSD roster and the census was never re-run.

**No portrait stopped rendering, and that is proven rather than asserted.**
`git diff a606659..HEAD` over `officeholders-us/04/33/34.json`,
`roster-photos.json` and `official-photos.json` is EMPTY — every input to the
partition is byte-identical to before F01, so nothing's reachability could have
moved.

**Item 2 — the count is 50, not 55.** The F01 brief was recovered from the
session transcript and the walkthrough document from git (`be0a590^`), so the
numbering is read rather than guessed. Sean's namespace holds **46 decimal
numbers (1.1 – 13.2), 0a/0b/0c, and the address addition — 50 rows.** No number
is missing and none is duplicated, and every distinct finding in the walkthrough
maps onto one, so nothing is unrepresented. The "fifty-five" counts spoken
findings at a finer grain than the numbering collapses them to — the meetings
order is raised twice, the gap language three times. **46 finished · 3 boundary
· 1 withdrawn · 0 never reached**, summing to 50. The three boundary stops are
1.2, 2.2 and 4.2, resolved from F01's own double-listing: each shipped its
render with an honest named gap and left a data hunt behind it.

**Item 4 — the 186 subcommittee rows are not 186 subcommittees.** Enumerated,
not sampled: all 230 committee rows classified by id shape, name convention and
seat presence. 181 children, and **every one of them is a genuine subcommittee**
— 0 orphans, 0 name mismatches, 0 duplicates of a parent, 0 task forces, 0
working groups, 0 commissions. The **186 reconciles as 179 seated subcommittees
plus 7 seated parents** whose jurisdiction is absent upstream, and those 7 are
all five joint bodies plus both House select committees. Upstream carries
jurisdiction for standing committees only, which is a fact about the source's
shape rather than a gap in our retrieval.

### A floor stops being a number

**Item 3.** F01 diagnosed the Kearsarge regression correctly — the snapshot held
all fifteen sittings and the oldest had reached the ninety-day back edge of the
serving window — and then wrote `14`, which is the same defect one day fresher.
It would have gone red again on 2026-09-02 when 2026-06-04 aged out, and again <!-- expected-future: the date the old fixed floor would next have gone red -->
in October. **The expectation is computed now**, every run, from the snapshot the
deploy is serving and the server's own window constants, mirrored from
`lib/meetings/query.ts`. `least` keeps only the durable half of the claim
(Kearsarge's sittings are on the board, plural) and the computed half carries the
precision — together strictly stronger than the old fifteen, because `least`
catches rows vanishing from the data and the expectation catches any row the
window admits failing to reach the reader. The staleness guard is the other half:
when the deploy's snapshot stamp is not the one on disk it reports COULD NOT RUN
with both stamps, never a red.

The second stale check needed nothing. The `0814c` ballot device-only checks were
already retired in F01 and replaced under the `F01` identity; the brief's premise
that both were left armed holds for the floor alone.

### The reader's own ballot was counting half of itself

**Item 8.** A pick can be arrived at two ways: a tap on the pick control, or a
Yes on the reaction control above it, which M134 derives a pick from. The
per-contest control resolved both; **the "My picks" list read the explicit file
alone.** The consequence fell along a line that matters — a MEASURE has no
measure-level reaction, because reactions attach to provisions, so a measure pick
can only ever be explicit and was always counted, while a CANDIDATE carries a
reaction target and was often not. The author found it from the outside: *"the
tally counts state ballot measures only."*

Two surfaces counted picks and both were fed that list, which is the defect
rather than an aggravation of it. They converge on `lib/ballot/pick-tally.ts`,
which the per-contest control also resolves through, so the two cannot disagree
about what a pick is. The denominator is built by the page's own
`pickOptionsFor` — the same builder all three `PickControl` call sites render
from — so M is the rendered row count by construction rather than by a second
query free to disagree with the page it sits on.

**Item 9.** "Clear my picks" emptied the explicit file, so the card vanished and
every derived pick went on standing underneath it. A control a reader reads as a
delete has to be one. The suppression lives in the picks file rather than in the
reaction record, and that is not timidity: `wtp.reactions` is the device's copy
of answers it has already sent, it exists so a reader can CHANGE one, and
deleting it would take that away while removing nothing from the anonymous
totals — which the capture notice already says cannot be un-joined.

**The four-zip walk caught a defect in the fix.** The first draft resolved the
suppression against the reader's stored picks, so a contest holding both an
explicit pick and a Yes came back EXPLICIT, escaped suppression, and re-derived
the Yes the instant the file was emptied. It failed on all four pilot zips with
"Your pick for this race: Katie Hobbs" still standing. A clear removes the
explicit picks, so the state to suppress is the state that exists after they are
gone.

Verified at 430×932 on the four pilot zips, all 32 checks green: 85701 N=2 of
M=20, 85641 2 of 20, 07866 2 of 6, 03255 2 of 12; every zip's M equals its
rendered pick controls, N equals its rendered rows, and after a clear no surface
reflects a pick — including after a reload, which is where a suppression living
in React state would have shown.

### A name with one token in it

**Item 10.** Vail Unified's superintendent was carried as "Carruth". A bare
surname is not a partial answer, it is a confident one: a reader cannot tell it
from a mononym, cannot search for the person, and cannot see that we are unsure.
Nothing in this product had ever been asked the question. `pnpm names:census`
asks it of all **1,369 people held — 0 incomplete names**, with the breakdown by
kind and state and the flagged rows printed per person, because a mononym is a
per-row ruling and nothing in the data marks one.

Running the detector found two defects in the detector. It stripped honorifics
and suffixes across the whole string, so "J.D." matched the Juris Doctor pattern
and flagged **J.D. Mesnard** and **J.D. Bernardy** — two sitting legislators who
publish themselves that way — as half-named; honorifics come off the front and
suffixes off the back now. And the census read the statewide executives' outer
row instead of their holder and reported three governors as nameless, which is a
census reporting what it could not read as a finding about the data.

**Vail's root cause is none of the three the brief proposed as likely.** Measured:
the home page's static HTML already links `/page/superintendent`, so discovery was
never blind; that page answers **200 to a plain fetch**, so no browser was needed;
and its HTML holds "John Carruth" six times, including
`<strong>John Carruth<br>Superintendent</strong>`. The fetch and the discovery both
worked and **the extraction failed** — the district runs on **Apptegy**, which ships
page content as an escaped JSON payload embedded in the HTML, so reading the
rendered prose finds a news blurb saying "Superintendent Carruth" and never the
byline. Rung 7 in miniature: the page's own data was right there and better than
its prose. The class is **2, not large** — 2 of 19 wiring rows are `APPTEGY` — and
it is bounded to person hunts, because the meetings adapter already reads that
site's own events API.

### The extraction was reading CMS templates as candidate speech

**Item 11**, and it is a correctness and neutrality defect rather than a
formatting one. Analilia Mejia was credited with health care and prescription
costs on the strength of a press-release index rail — a list of links, beginning
mid-word. A candidate whose site carries a "Read More" rail gets credited with
issues they never addressed while a candidate on a simpler site shows "mentions 0
of them", which is an information asymmetry **the product manufactures itself**
inside a live contest.

Three independent means, in `lib/text/boilerplate.ts`: structural exclusion
before extraction on every site; a repetition test over pages of the same site;
and a passage-level reading, because a rail inside `<main>` with no marking
defeats both of the others. **The repetition test could not run anywhere** — all
51 sites hold fewer than three pages — so structural exclusion stood alone on 51
of 51, and that is stated rather than implied. RULING 9 is enforced where the
passage is CREATED, so chrome cannot feed the tally either; filtering the display
and not the count would leave the asymmetry in the number being sold while hiding
it from the reader.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| quotations | 113 | 101 (12 withdrawn) |
| issue mentions (candidate × issue) | 72 | 64 (−8) |
| quotations beginning or ending mid-word | **113** | **0** |

Eight of 49 candidates' counts moved and every one moved DOWN — Biggs 1→0, Swing
3→2, Ciscomani 3→2, Grijalva 1→0, Pappas 4→3, Selen 2→1, Mejia 2→1, Booker 1→0.
That direction is the correct outcome and is reported as a correction.

**A defect in the fix, caught by measuring rather than by reasoning.** The first
marker list matched substrings anywhere in an attribute, so `menu` hit 263
containers on `azleg.gov` and the strip took a page from 7,652 extracted
characters to 25 — the same asymmetry wearing the other face. Markers match whole
class tokens now.

**And the corpus needed a new field to survive the change.** It is keyed on the
hash of its own extracted text, so stripping chrome would have reported 59
campaigns revising their positions on a day none did — destroying the one signal
that carries this product's accountability half by using it for something else.
`extractorVersion` distinguishes "they changed the page" from "we got better at
reading it": the re-collection reports **0 revisions and 30 re-extractions**, and
`currentExtraction` supersedes an older-extractor copy for READING while the file
stays append-only.

### Two defects found in passing, both instruments lying quietly

* **`components/ballot/pick-control.tsx` carried two literal NUL bytes** — a join
  separator written as the character. **ripgrep classifies such a file as binary
  and SKIPS it**, so every class sweep of this codebase silently missed a
  ballot-surface file, on the surface four of this session's items live on. Any
  sweep run against this repo before 2026-08-19 did not see that file.
* **`scripts/photo-census.mts` dated its own document in UTC** and wrote
  2026-08-20 at 18:19 on 2026-08-19 — the smaller sibling `CLAUDE.md`'s date rule <!-- expected-future: the wrong date the UTC bug produced, quoted as evidence -->
  names, in a script nothing audited.

Both are the same family as the two the reconciliations found: an instrument
reporting confidently about something it was not measuring.

### Two existing tests corrected, both wrong rather than newly broken

`D05` asserted `attempted >= documents.length`, which append-only guarantees will
break the first time a second run appends (68 attempted, 96 documents). And the
`P02` headline test took the first candidate key in document order, which after
the strip is a candidate whose only page is a JS shell — it was reading the
NOTHING_COLLECTED sentence and calling that a failure of the other one.

## F01-continued session 2 — 2026-08-19: the ballot stops being a wall, and four instruments stop lying about what they measured

Session 1 finished items 1 through 11 and never reached 12 through 17. This
session is those six, plus four closures of questions session 1 opened. **Ten
items, ten finished.** F01 closes.

The through-line is not "we found bugs." It is that in six of the ten, **the
thing that was wrong was an instrument reporting confidently about something
it had not measured** — a sweep run with a tool that skips, a search reading a
different corpus, a fetch recording a challenge page as a document, a reach map
that could not see a surface, a guard whose ID check was defeated by a broken
row boundary, and a walk check counting content on a row it had just been moved
off. The code, in most of those, was fine.

### The ballot was forty-four screens

**Item 12.** Every long section rendered inline under every candidate while the
large battlecard sat with slots for them. Measured at 430×932 before touching
anything, and — this matters — the BEFORE was taken against **production**, on
`d722605`, at the identical figure to the local build, so the baseline is the
shipped state rather than a development artifact.

| zip | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 07866 | 20,510 px · **22.0 phone screens** | 9,574 px · **10.3** |
| 85701 | 41,558 px · **44.6 screens** | 31,298 px · **33.6** |

Three sections moved — "in their own words", campaign money, the incumbent
record door — and the row keeps portrait, name, party, the short sourced line,
the links row, a one-line count and a full-width **View Battlecard** pill.
Class swept across all four pilot zips: **107 candidate rows, 107 pills, 0
inline positions, 0 inline funding** (85701 20/20, 85641 25/25, 07866 15/15,
03255 47/47).

**The card is new, and the reason is the equal-effort rule rather than
convenience.** `OfficialModal` is the existing large person surface and it
already carries every slot the moved sections need. It is also built from a
`SeatHolder`, which comes from the exact-key incumbent join — so **it only
opens for an incumbent.** Moving the sections there would have deleted a
CHALLENGER's own words and funding block in every contest while leaving the
incumbent's. That is not a layout regression; it is `CLAUDE.md`'s "the app can
say nothing about anyone and still tilt a race", wearing a tidiness argument.
`CandidateBattlecard` takes children instead, so every candidate gets the
identical pill opening the identical card, with whatever we actually hold
inside — including, honestly, very little.

**People only, structurally.** The pill is a slot on `CandidateCard`, and a
measure renders through the measure path and never reaches that component.

**The reaction and pick controls stay inline, and the decision is recorded
rather than assumed.** They are not long sections; they have no candidate
battlecard slot; and burying the revenue path changes what gets captured, which
`CLAUDE.md`'s "Ask before" list reserves to the author. The tension with
"reactions are always asked after the explanation" is real, and it is answered
by the row keeping the sourced line and the blurb above the control with the
fuller explanation one tap above it.

### The search was reading a different corpus, not an empty one

**Item 13.** The brief offered four causes and it is the third — **a
differently-shaped record.** This product holds TWO statement corpora:

| file | rows | keyed by | read by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data/corpus/statements.json` | 32 snapshots, 22 subjects | OFFICEHOLDER id | the battlecard's Positions search |
| `data/candidates/corpus-2026.json` | 96 documents, 49 candidates | CANDIDATE key | the ballot's "in their own words" |

`PositionsSection` was handed a subject id and searched the first. Every
candidate whose words live only in the second was **absent from the index**, so
the search answered — honestly, for the corpus it had — *"we haven't collected
anything they've published"*, four inches below that candidate's published
words. Nothing was broken; two stores drifted and one surface knew about one.

The index is the UNION now: **32 + 66 = 98 snapshots over 71 subjects, 79

### Two found in passing, and both were quiet

**A bot-detection interstitial served at HTTP 200 was being recorded as a
successful read of an empty page** — in `politeGetText`, the one function every
adapter fetches through. Apptegy's edge does not refuse an unfamiliar client;
it answers `200 OK` with a 3,036-byte "Client Challenge" page. Measured: curl
gets 259,887 bytes where undici gets 3,036. **Nothing defeats a challenge** —
the request is re-issued through the client the host serves unchallenged, which
is rung 4 as written, and if that is challenged too it THROWS naming the wall.
The first run of the embedded-JSON census reported **0 of 95 sites clean**
because of this, and that number is recorded in the ladder because it is the
exact shape of a false all-clear.

broken record boundary defeats an ID check silently.

## F22 — 2026-08-20: the refresh was red on a path separator, and one vendor timeout emptied a township

**The reader-facing fact first: the meetings snapshot stopped moving at
2026-08-18T18:59Z and did not move again until this session.** For roughly
forty-two hours the live site served meetings data that was two days stale,
four scheduled refreshes ran and committed nothing, and every one of them
reported red without anyone reading why.

### The brief's premise was wrong in a way worth recording

The brief said two runs had failed — #30 and #31 — and that "everything before
them on `main` is green, including build checks #73 through #78." The run list
says otherwise: **#27, #28, #29, #30 and #31 all failed, and #25 and #26 were
cancelled at the six-hour job limit.** The last successful run was **#23, on
2026-08-18T18:58Z.**

And the second half of that premise is the interesting half, because it is
true and misleading at the same time. The build checks WERE green.
`.github/workflows/build-check.yml` runs `pnpm build` and the bundle budgets
and **never runs `pnpm test`.** The four scheduled refresh gates are this
repository's **only Linux runner of the suite.** A test that passes on Windows
and fails on Linux is therefore invisible everywhere except in the jobs that
keep the reader's data current — which is where it surfaced, wearing a
data-pipeline costume.

### The ingest was never the failure

This was worth establishing before touching anything, because the obvious
story — a data job is red, so the data source must be broken — was false.

In every failing run the ingest step **exited 0**, named its walls, and
carried forward correctly. Run #30: `10/11 sources`, `civicplus: FAILED —
civicplus timed out after 20000ms`, `40 meeting(s) CARRIED FORWARD`. Run #31:
`11/11 sources`, 23 carried. The governed artifact CHANGED on every run, so
the gate ran — and **the gate is what failed.**

### Cause one: a path separator, and a guard that got stricter instead of failing

`tests/coverage-manifest.test.ts` shipped on 2026-08-18 with AUD-06. Its
allowlist of fourteen legitimate per-state content files was mapped through
`.replace(/\//g, "\\")` and then matched against `relative()` — which yields
backslashes on Windows and forward slashes on POSIX. On Linux **nothing was
allowlisted**, so every content table reported itself an offender.

The proof is in the offender list the CI log printed: it contains
`lib/coverage/states.ts`, **the manifest the allowlist exists to exempt.** A
file cannot be an offender against itself; the list had simply stopped
matching.

The fix normalizes repo-relative paths to POSIX at the single place they are
produced. The more useful half is the second guard: **"every allowlisted
content file is a file the sweep actually reaches."** A broken exemption list
does not fail — it gets STRICTER, which is why this read as fourteen new
offenders rather than as a broken test. That guard fails on either platform,
naming the entry.

### Cause two: civicplus never declared its archive, so a timeout deleted a township's history

Run #30 failed a second test: `only 23 day-only meetings in the snapshot —
M59 ingested 27`. That one is the g13 Merrimack defect of 2026-08-18,
**repeating on a second adapter.**

`lib/meetings/carry-forward.ts` judges a walled source's carried rows against
that source's own `publishedLookbackDays`, defaulting to
`CONCLUDED_LOOKBACK_DAYS` = 90. civicplus's M59 AgendaCenter rung — shipped
`269a3ce` on 2026-08-15, three days BEFORE revize declared its own — emits
every dated sitting the archive lists and clips nothing off the back. It never
declared that. So when civicplus timed out, carry-forward clipped its archive
at ninety days.

**The arithmetic closes exactly.** A sweep of the committed snapshot by source
against a 90-day back edge: 11 sources, **2** emit rows beyond the window —
revize (15 rows, 7 older, back to 2026-02-09, declared) and civicplus (52
rows, **23** older, back to 2026-01-06, undeclared). Run #30 logged
`Rockaway Township, NJ 9` where the committed snapshot held 32. **32 − 9 =
23**, the exact count of civicplus rows older than ninety days.

One vendor's twenty-second timeout deleted two thirds of a New Jersey
township's published meeting history, and then turned the whole four-times-daily
refresh red so that ten healthy sources could not commit their fresh data
either.

The guard for it is **derived, not listed** — a hand-kept list of archive
adapters is the same shape of thing that failed. It asks the committed
snapshot which sources emit rows past the default back edge and holds each to
a declaration reaching its own oldest row. **It was proved able to fail:** with
the declaration removed it reports `civicplus (oldest row 2026-01-06, declared
window 90d)`; with it restored, green.

### Cause three, and it was ours: the batch job was using the reader's stopwatch

The timeout itself was not a vendor refusing us. `CompositeSource` defaults to
a 20-second per-source budget, which is right for the live map — a reader is
waiting. `pnpm ingest composite` was silently borrowing it. civicplus
serializes an iCal GET and an AgendaCenter GET per wired body at the polite
spacing every adapter honours, and ran past twenty seconds. **Nothing refused
us; we hung up.**

`SCHEDULED_REFRESH_TIMEOUT_MS` (120s) now applies to the scheduled ingest
only. No request rate changed and no politeness changed.

### A wall and a broken job are two different kinds of nothing

`ok: false` carried a vendor timeout and a violated id-namespace contract in
the same flag, and `scripts/ingest.ts` treated both identically: name it, skip
it, carry its rows, exit 0. So **a defect in our own code rendered as a walled
vendor and kept the run green** — the failed-operation-as-empty-success shape
wearing its other face. And the converse cost more: because everything was a
wall, nothing could be a job failure, so the exit status said nothing at all.

* **`WALL`** — the retrieval did not land. Named, skipped, rows carried, run
  continues. Ten healthy sources must not lose their refresh over one vendor's
  edge.
* **`JOB`** — a child returned ids outside its namespace, or its `normalize`
  threw. No rung of the ladder fixes it and no wall fell. The run goes red.

The wall record carries **the ladder rung it stopped at**, in `CLAUDE.md`'s
existing numbering and not a parallel vocabulary: `SourceHttpError` now knows
whether it stopped at rung 2 (plain fetch), 3 (full browser header set) or 4
(a different TLS client). **Absent stays absent** — a whole-child timeout
knows no rung and prints as `unrecorded` rather than being given a plausible
number. `SOURCE_BLOCKED` remains prohibited and no terminal state was added.

Every run now prints, unconditionally:

```
RUN SUMMARY: 11 source(s) attempted, 11 read, 0 walled, 0 job-failed, 314 row(s) written
```

### The class, swept

**Four** scheduled workflows fetch external sources —
`refresh-meetings-snapshot`, `refresh-dotgov-snapshot`, `refresh-fec-snapshot`,
`refresh-legiscan-snapshot`. All four gate on the identical full
`corepack pnpm test`, so **one fix converged four.** Only the meetings refresh
was actively red; the other three were **latent** — their artifacts happened
not to move, so each took the "unchanged, gate skipped" path and reported
success. `tests/workflow-actions.test.ts` now enumerates the four and asserts
each gates on the full suite from the changed path, so a fifth cannot be added
without one.

The three single-artifact refreshes were checked rather than assumed:
`scripts/fetch-dotgov.mts` already refuses to write a thin snapshot and throws.
For a single-source refresh, "walled" and "read nothing" are the same event, so
going red is correct and already the behaviour.

Item 6's both-places rule of 2026-08-15 was right while the two were LINKS in
different context; item 15 made both the same in-app pill, and a repeated

Two guards carried the number 2 and **both were amended with their old text

### What is NOT fixed, and is named rather than guessed at

**F25 — two scheduled runs hung and were cancelled at the six-hour limit.**
Runs #25 (6h0m22s) and #26 (6h48m10s) both reached the gate and produced no

not reproducing and it is not fixed.** Next rung recorded: a `timeout-minutes`
on the gate step in all four refresh workflows, so a hang costs minutes and
reports as a hang rather than costing six hours and reporting as a
cancellation.

## Prompt B — ingest, the national denominator, coverage tiers, and the tracker (2026-08-20)

**All eleven items finished.** The session's deliverable is
`data/derived/gap-ledger.md`. *(Moved to `docs/gap-ledger.md` on 2026-08-20 by
Prompt E item 11 — a person looking for where the project stands does not open
`data/derived`. The sentence above is left as Prompt B wrote it; this note is
the pointer, not a rewrite.)*

**Ships.** One planned code merge, PR
[#116](https://github.com/SeanJ22/We-The-People/pull/116), merged as
**`3bc8834`**, which is what `/api/build` reports production serving. The
branch carried eight commits and they landed together; **there was no second
code merge**, and the only exception RULING 1 permits was not used. Close-out
records follow as their own commits, per the rule that a document cannot name
the commit containing it.

### What replaced the coverage number

The product reported coverage against its own registry. That number always
looked good and meant nothing, because a registry that defines its own
denominator cannot be caught missing anything. Three real denominators now
stand behind every claim:

* **47,834 of 90,837** Census governments resolve to at least one zip (52.66%).
* **39,555 of 39,555** special districts are **UNRESOLVED** — 43.55% of every
  government in the country, and TIGER publishes no boundary for a single one
  at any vintage.
* **33,075 of 33,791 zips sit at Tier 0** (97.88%), 716 at Tier 1, none higher.

The 97.88% is the honest number and the first draft of the stamper did not
produce it. It set `universeGovernments = territoryResolved`, which makes Tier 1
true by construction everywhere and printed **99.71% Tier 1** — the
self-referential denominator this whole model exists to replace, reintroduced
inside the model. The universe includes the special districts; a zip's tier is
the **floor** across the governments touching it; one unresolved government
drops the zip, because that is exactly the government a reader might live under
and hear nothing about.

### Three class defects found by reading output rather than trusting it

1. **TIGER pseudo-entities are not governments.** 85641 resolved to
   `School District Not Defined` [0499997]. TIGER tiles its layers without holes
   using reserved local codes 99997/99998/99999. **27 excluded**, named on every
   run.
2. **Statistical entities are not governments.** **12,587 of 32,608** `place`
   rows are CDPs and **5,198 of 36,367** `cousub` rows are CCDs. Neither has a
   council, a budget, a meeting or an elected official. Every edge now carries
   `GOVERNMENT` / `STATISTICAL` / `UNCLASSIFIED` with its LSAD — and the third
   value is the point, because a New England gore is not guessed into either
   bucket. **216,146** government edges, 42,407 statistical, 13,973 unclassified.
3. **The DBF reader guessed its encoding.** It hardcoded `latin1` while every
   Census boundary zip ships a `.cpg` declaring UTF-8, so the join wrote a Texas
   place name as mojibake. Caught by this repo's own `tests/mojibake.test.ts`,
   which then caught the *comment* explaining the fix for pasting the broken
   spelling in as an example. The encoding is now **read from the file**.

### The crosswalk's low match rate was a finding about the normalizer

The first draft matched **2,038 of 13,859** and that number said nothing about
the data. Census writes `CASTRO VAL UNIFIED SCH DIST` where CCD writes
`Castro Valley Unified`. With abbreviation expansion, acronym expansion and
structural-token removal it matches **9,776**. A join that returns almost
nothing looks identical to a universe that genuinely does not overlap, and only
opening the unmatched rows tells them apart.

### The ledger would not have existed on production

`lib/coverage/zip-tier.ts` builds its path with `process.cwd()`, which Next
cannot resolve statically, so the file would simply not have been in the deploy.
The read would have thrown, the catch would have returned null, and **every zip
would have rendered "we have not worked this ZIP code out yet" while every sold
row was stamped `UNKNOWN`** — the surface's own honest gap wording. A broken
deploy and honest missing data are the same pixels.

Two files now, written in one pass from the same values: the 18 MB audit ledger
stays in the repo, and a **666 KB** runtime copy is traced into the five routes
that read it. Verified in the built manifests and against the live site, not
assumed.

### The Linux gate caught something on its first run

RULING 13 said a green build check did not mean the tests ran. `build-check.yml`
grew a `gates` job. Its first run went red, and what it caught was **not this
session's work**: `tsc --noEmit` has never been runnable on a clean checkout,
because `tsconfig.json` includes `.next/types/**` and `LayoutProps` is generated
by the build. It passes on a developer's machine because `.next` is lying around
from the last build. Reproduced locally by moving `.next` aside — same error, on
Windows, so not a platform difference. The type check now runs **after** the
build, and the suite asserts that order.

column with no default may only lose its default once the code that fills it is

without hand-editing the journal.

### F11's extraction toolkit, and the layer that is why it exists

Four layers under one contract: **a zero-row extraction is a failed extraction,
never an empty document**, enforced inside the constructor rather than left to
every caller. `EXTRACTED` / `ZERO_ROWS` / `CANNOT_RUN` are three answers, and
the last two are deliberately different — a scanned agenda recorded as a
document that published nothing is a false claim about a public body.

### RULING 26, 27 and 28 are law

`CLAUDE.md` went **60,928 → 65,046 bytes**. There is no size cap on it.

**RULING 26 — SHOW EVERYTHING WE FIND**, with its rationale attached in full,
because a stripped rule reads as guidance. Completeness is a property of the
HUNT and kept being treated as a property of the record. Every version of the
gate — strict field equality in Prompt B, hunt-completion equality in Prompt C —
tried to make the display responsible for a fairness problem that belongs to the
collection discipline, and each withheld more than the last. Equal effort lives
in the hunt: a hunt session takes a contest as a unit and works every candidate
in it before moving on. It is not a display rule and it never becomes one.

**RULING 27 — no suppression path may exist**, guarded by
`tests/no-suppression.test.ts`, which fails the build rather than waiting for
the author to open the site. That is how both previous versions were found.

**RULING 28 — one buried annotation per contest.** The exact wording shipped:

> **\* An incumbent is likely to have more information available here than the
> people running against them.**

In DOM order it sits **after the candidate `<ul>` and before the state-funding
note and the pick control**, in `text-muted` at `0.6875rem`. The marker is a
bare `<sup>*</sup>` on the contest heading, not a link — the footnote is a few
centimetres below it inside the same card, and a jump link to something already
on screen is reader friction with nothing to buy it.

`docs/rulings.md` (14,390 → 23,961 bytes before this section) records RULING 7's
display half and RULING 18 as **DEAD, superseded in full**, with what each was

### The six federal members, named

`docs/officials-audit.md` has said "531 division-linked of 537" since
2026-08-14 with nothing saying what the six were. A stated number with an
unexplained remainder is a margin, and a margin is where a real loss hides.

All six are **non-voting**: Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC), Stacey E. Plaskett (VI),
Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen (AS), James C. Moylan (GU) and Kimberlyn
King-Hinds (MP) are Delegates; Pablo José Hernández (PR) is the Resident
Commissioner. **Not a vacancy, not a resignation, not a join loss.**

The mechanism, stated separately from the classification: each carries a
division of the shape `…/state:<xx>/cd:at-large`, `lib/registry` holds no such
division because the district geometry comes from Census TIGER congressional
districts which do not enumerate DC or the five territories, and
`scripts/build-officeholders.ts` **correctly** drops the link and records it in
`unmatched` with the id it looked for. The join works; the divisions do not
exist. The arithmetic: 537 = 100 senators + 437 House; 437 = 431 voting reps + 6
non-voting; 531 = 100 + 431; four House seats vacant on the read date.

`tests/federal-roster.test.ts` names the six and fails if a seventh appears
unexplained, if one of them becomes division-linked without leaving the list, or
if the counts stop reconciling. `scripts/audit-officials.mts` prints the
unlinked members with their recorded reason, so the document carries the named
remainder from its next generation. The reader consequence — nobody in six
territories can reach their own member from a division lookup — is **`PD01`**.

### `D73`: the class, not the instance

**The schema gate.** `app/api/schema/route.ts` asks the RUNNING DEPLOY whether
the database it talks to has the migrations it was built from. Per request,
uncached, **HTTP 503 with the missing migration named by tag**; 501 when there
is no database to ask and 502 when the migrations table could not be read,
because an unreadable answer must never print as a passing one. Not at build
time (the builder has no production credential) and not at cold start (a cached
answer would report "in sync" through the entire window the gate exists to
catch). Mirrored by `pnpm db:check` for CI, wired **read-only** into the daily
intake-tripwire workflow ahead of the tripwire step, and asserted by walk:all.
A gate that could fix what it finds would apply an unreviewed migration to
production at 4am, so it names and refuses.

It found something on its first run, before it had shipped: **the local Neon
branch is eight migrations behind** (`PD02`). Production was one behind — the
brand-new `0015`, applied before the code that writes to it went out, which is
the ordering D73 got wrong. Production is now **16 of 16**.

**The write alarm.** A failed write to `search_log` or `reactions` raises into
`write_alarm` — its own space, the same discipline `intake_limiter` carries: no
zip, no division, no continuity key, no run id, no foreign key, no column that
could join to any store. It holds the store, the SQLSTATE and the database's own
words. Readable by `pnpm alarms`, asserted by walk:all, read daily by the
tripwire workflow.

**RULING 25 held throughout.** Every reader-facing status and body on all three
sold-store write paths is byte-identical to what shipped before, pinned in
`tests/write-alarm.test.ts`.

**The sweep.** Exactly **three** call sites write to a sold store —
`app/api/meetings`, `app/api/reactions`, `app/api/log` — derived from source
rather than hand-listed, so a fourth joins the guard on its first test run. All
three raise. Of the 25 catch sites in `app/`, the rest are not sold-store
writes; `lib/db/feedback.ts` and `lib/db/intake-limiter.ts` already return
failure rather than success. **Count found 3, count fixed 3.** One adjacent
finding was recorded rather than fixed: `PD03`, a failed division lookup writing
an empty `ocdIds` list onto a reaction row.

### The two things the live verification caught, and both are in the record

**Second code merge.** The alarm fired as `void raiseWriteAlarm(...)` with the
response returned on the next line. A serverless invocation ends when the
response goes out and a promise still in flight is dropped, so the induced
failure got its correct 400 and **nothing landed**. Every test passed. The alarm
built to catch a silent failure failed silently. `/api/log` and `/api/reactions`
now await it; `/api/meetings` schedules it with `after()`. Guarded: a bare
`void raiseWriteAlarm(` is banned. That import broke two test files —
`next/server` is a real file with no `exports` map, so node RESOLVED the
specifier and then failed to LOAD it — and `scripts/test-alias-loader.mjs` now
learns what the bundler already knows.

**Third code merge, and it is a deviation from the one-merge rule, named as
one.** The alarm's first REAL firing wrote a row reading `Failed query: insert
into "search_log" (…) params: …,03255,["ocd-division/country:us/state:nh/…`. The
Neon driver wraps a failure as the query plus its **params**, so the message
carried a reader's zip and the divisions their search resolved to, into the one
table whose entire design is that it holds nothing about who was writing. The
column guard cannot see a value smuggled inside a text field it permits.
`errorMessageOf` now cuts at `params:` and scrubs division- and zip-shaped
tokens from what survives; `column "coverage_tier" does not exist` — the
sentence that would have closed D73 in a minute — is untouched by either. The
one offending row was deleted, named: `e2e0d8ff-5ae8-4c96-838f-97b18bad4b2b`,
raised `2026-08-21T00:21:13.729Z`, store `search_log`. It went because its <!-- expected-future: a real UTC instant read from write_alarm; the Phoenix day was 2026-08-20 and UTC had already turned over -->
CONTENTS are not permitted, not because the finding was inconvenient.

### The alarm is raising true positives

Two separate walk runs each raised exactly one `search_log` alarm —
`2026-08-21T00:21:13Z` and `2026-08-21T00:28:19Z` — with **no SQLSTATE** on <!-- expected-future: real UTC instants read from write_alarm; the Phoenix day was 2026-08-20 and UTC had already turned over -->
either, which points at a transport failure rather than a database refusal. The
first run landed 93 + 9 rows, so the rate is on the order of **one insert in
ninety-four**. `search_log` is a sold store; a one-percent loss is invisible to
every reader and shows up in a buyer's aggregate as a number slightly smaller
than the truth. **Nobody could have known this before the alarm existed.**
`PD04` holds it. The standing walk check is RED on it and is correct to be.

### The queue model, and who may move a row

`docs/tracker.xlsx` is the workbook the author edits: **Working**, **Resolved**,
and a **How to use this** tab explaining the columns, the three resolution
states, and how to add a row. It opens and edits normally in Excel and Google
Sheets — verified by reading the shipped file back through .NET's own `ZipFile`
and through this repo's reader, and by a round trip in which a note, a
resolution and a brand-new blank-id row all survived, including a 13,211-character
session record byte for byte.

**Three columns are the author's** — `Resolution`, `Condition`, `Notes` — and a
session never writes them. `corepack pnpm tracker:move` reads them back out of
the workbook and into the stores; nothing else writes the workbook.

**Collision safety:** the workbook is digested when it is read and digested again
immediately before it is written. A difference means he saved it mid-run, and the
run **refuses and writes nothing**, names the file, and says to run it again.
The committed CSVs are what every other script and test reads, so a session that
never runs the move script cannot collide with him at all.

**RULING 37 and RULING 41 are guarded in both directions.** A session may not
resolve or move a *Needs Sean* row; the same resolution in his handwriting does
move. A session may not reword, retitle or delete a row he wrote; it may work it
and set a priority if none is set. Both are pure functions in
`scripts/tracker-core.mjs` so the guard and the script cannot drift apart, and
`tests/tracker-stores.test.ts` fails the build on either.

### `PD04` — the one lost insert in ninety, closed

**Two defects, both ours, both on the write path only.** The reader-facing catch
is unchanged (RULING 25) and the responses are byte-identical.

1. **The loss.** `app/api/meetings/route.ts` called `logSearchEvent()` and never
   awaited it and never handed it to `after()`, then returned its JSON on the
   next line. On a serverless runtime the invocation ends when the response is
   returned and a promise still in flight is dropped — **silently, without
   rejecting, so no `.catch` could ever see it.** Prompt D fixed exactly this
   shape for the ALARM and left the INSERT five lines above it.
2. **The instrument.** `lib/db/write-alarm.ts` read `.code` and `.message` off
   the object it was handed. Drizzle hands it a `DrizzleQueryError`, whose own
   source carries no `code` and whose message is the SQL. So the alarm recorded
   **SQLSTATE `null` for every query failure structurally**, and recorded the
   statement where the reason should be. Both now walk the `.cause` chain.

**Ruled out with evidence:** a constraint violation (the table carries only
`NOT NULL`s and a generated primary key — no unique, check or foreign key is
reachable) and a retry path reporting success (there is none, at either call
site). **Ruled in:** the dropped promise, structurally.

**Proved as a pair on the live deploy:** 200 declared synthetic GETs, run id
`promptE-writeproof@2026-08-21T02:55:00Z`, window 02:41:21Z–02:42:06Z. <!-- expected-future: a run id and window minted in UTC; the Phoenix day was 2026-08-20 and UTC had already turned over -->
**Attempted 200 · landed 200 · loss 0 of 200 (0.00%) · 0 alarms raised.**

### The live regression, and the sixth sighting of a shape

The close-out walk found `M123` red. The 02:00Z scheduled refresh had reported
the `ical` source as `ok: true, fetched: 3, normalized: 0` with **every drop
counter at zero** — three documents in hand, not one event out of them, and no
drop to account for one. Because the source reported success, **carry-forward
never ran**, and Wilmot went from 23 meetings to none.

`CLAUDE.md`: *a zero-row extraction is a FAILED extraction, never an empty
document.* Sixth sighting, first to reach a reader.

**WALL or JOB, and half of it is not determinable.** The feed was healthy when
fetched by hand minutes later — HTTP 200, 20 events, categories intact — and a
local re-run read 3 fetched, 23 normalized. So what the CI runner received at
02:00Z was not the calendar, and whether that was an egress served a different
page (a wall at rung 5) or a transient empty response **cannot be recovered; the
bytes are gone.** Both readings are stated rather than one being chosen. What is
ours, and is what shipped, is that the composite recorded it as success.

**Fixed at the shared code path**, not in the adapter it was found in: all
eleven children pass through one line in `lib/sources/composite/index.ts`, and
only `ical` had any notion of a refusal of its own — **class swept, 1 found, 1
fixed, at a path covering 11.** The tension is stated in the code rather than
hidden: a body that genuinely goes quiet is marked red too, which is the correct
trade in this direction, because carried rows are clipped to the serving window
and age out within days while a silently emptied town is wrong on screen
immediately. A source that fetched and DROPPED everything is left alone.

Snapshot regenerated: **318 meetings from 11/11 sources, Wilmot back at 23**,
1 row carried. The walk after the fix reads *68 meeting(s) across 4
jurisdiction(s)* at 03255.

## NH Hunt — 2026-08-20: the zero-row shape is made inexpressible, and Newbury's own calendar turns out to have been there all along

**This is the first session that put DEPTH on the site.** Items 1, 2, 2b, 3, 4,
7, 8 and 9 finished. Item 5 — the bodies — ran until the session was out of
room and is reported mid-list with the list stated. Item 6 — the 47 candidacies
— was not started, and where it stops is named at the foot of this section.

### What a reader at 03255 has that they did not have this morning

| At 03255 | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Bodies governing the point | 6 | **20** |
| — of those, ingested | 6 | **17** |
| Newbury town's own bodies | 4 | **17** |
| Meeting rows on the live map | 16 | **28** |
| Named officials with a sourced roster | 15 | **90** |
| Rosters at 03255 and its county | 3 | **13** |

Every one of those numbers is a body, a person or a sitting that a public body
had already published and this product could not see.

### The find, and it was a `webcal://` link on a page we had already read

`https://www.newbury.nh.gov/calendar/ical/export.ics` — **1,157 events**, 94 of
them upcoming, advertised by the town's own calendar page and wired to nothing.
Ten Newbury committees had no meetings route at all while their sittings sat in
a document the town publishes for exactly this purpose.

Four things had to be built or fixed before that file could reach a reader, and
each is a class fix rather than a Newbury fix:

1. **`titleMatch` in the `ical` adapter.** The feed carries no `CATEGORIES`
   field on any of its 1,157 events, and the adapter required one. A
   category-only reader sees a town publishing everything as a town publishing
   nothing. The match is a LIST, because a town spells its own bodies several
   ways — Newbury writes both "Supervisors of the Checklist" and "Supervisions
   of the Checklist", a typo it has repeated for years, and dropping the variant
   would drop the meetings.
2. **An empty `LOCATION` is not a placeless meeting.** D18's `placeless` means
   the body published a string naming no building. Newbury publishes no
   `LOCATION` line at all, and reading that silence as an assertion dropped
   twenty-four sittings before the row's own `venueMatch` was ever consulted.
3. **A 403 walks the ladder for every adapter.** The feed answers **403 to this
   process and 200 to `curl`, 467,525 bytes, with either User-Agent** — a
   TLS-fingerprint wall, ladder rung 4. The escalation existed and was reachable
   only from the browser profile, so every adapter that had not opted in stopped
   at rung 2 and called a serving feed a wall.
4. **One feed is fetched once.** Ten bodies on one URL meant ten requests for
   the same 466 KB per refresh. The town's reputation limiter started refusing
   pages it had served minutes earlier, which is a wall we built ourselves.

### The merge that had to exist before a second route could ship

The four Newbury boards that were already wired hold **24 in-window sittings on
the town's feed against the 16 their existing routes produce** — Selectboard 10
against 7, Planning 5 against 3, Zoning 4 against 1, Conservation 5 against 5.

Swapping was measured and REFUSED: the existing routes carry real agendas
(`newburynh.civicweb.net/Portal/MeetingInformation.aspx?Id=3370`,
`/planning-board/agenda/agenda-15`) and the feed carries none. Trading a
reader's agenda for a reader's date is not a trade this product should make.

So both ship and `collapseDuplicateSittings` decides. It keys on
`ocdId | bodyName | INSTANT` — the first version keyed on the string and
collapsed nothing at all, because `schedulepage` writes
`2026-06-16T19:00:00-04:00` and `ical` writes `2026-06-16T23:00:00.000Z` for the
same moment. It collapses ACROSS SOURCES ONLY, so a board publishing a Regular
and an Executive Session at one hour keeps both. It runs AGAIN after
carry-forward, because carry-forward restores rows the merge never saw — three
of Newbury's Conservation Commission sittings walked back in behind it on the
first refresh. **The snapshot states the collapse as its own number and the
pair reconciles**: 328 claimed by sources = 316 fresh + 12 collapsed.

### Item 1 — the sixth sighting closed in the type, not in a sixth rule

`normalizeWithDrops` returns a branded `Accounted<...>`. The only constructor is
`accountedNormalize()`, and it THROWS rather than returning a value for a
non-zero fetch with zero rows and zero drops. A plain object literal no longer
compiles; `tsc` names it at the `return`, in the adapter, at authorship time.
Twelve of twelve implementations converted.

**It caught a real one on its first live run**, which is the best thing that can
be said about a new contract: a fully refused `ical` source arrives as ten raw
rows, zero meetings, zero drops — a WALL, correctly reported by the adapter, and
the factory called it a broken parser. A refused row is not a document in hand,
so the factory takes `unretrieved`.

The six sightings, and whether the contract would have caught each:

| # | Sighting | Caught? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | An empty RSS feed recorded as working | **No** — a fetch layer, above this contract. |
| 2 | A zero-match join presented as a clean build | **No** — a build script, not an adapter. |
| 3 | A scripted edit that edited nothing and exited 0 | **No** — not an adapter at all. |
| 4 | A NovusAgenda portal returning 200 with zero meetings, recorded as a HIT | **Yes**, had it been an adapter on this contract. |
| 5 | An Apptegy page whose prose never held the byline | **No** — extraction, and layer 4 of the toolkit is what covers it. |
| 6 | `ical` fetched 3, normalized 0, and Wilmot lost 23 meetings | **Yes**, at compile time and again at run time. |

Two of six, and the honest reading is that this contract closes the ADAPTER
class exactly and nothing else. The other four live in the fetch layer, in build
scripts and in extraction — which is why the extraction toolkit carries the same
refusal in `extracted()`, and why the remaining two shapes are still only a
written rule.

### Items 2 and 2b — the guard gap was the defect

`positionsAnnotation`, `CandidatePositionsAnnotation`, `annotationSlot` and the
buried gap enumeration are gone from four files. `positionsHeadline` carries no
digit. A candidate we hold no published words for renders **no positions section
at all**. `CLAUDE.md`'s fourth friction exception is retired with the reason
attached.

The new guard matches MEANING — subject + absence + coverage lexicons — and
**proves it is not vacuous** by running the matcher against every such sentence
this product has actually shipped plus three rewrites nobody has written. Its
false negatives are stated in its own doc block: assembled sentences outside the
named files, vocabulary the lexicons do not know, non-sentence markers, and
context.

`Delete` is a fourth resolution state, his alone; `B08` is hard-removed from
both stores and recorded permanently. The RULING 48 hook refuses destructive git
against his four files — **it blocked one of my own commands, and then blocked
this session's own commit message**, which was a false positive, is fixed, and
is guarded with the commit message as a test case.

### What the hunt found that nobody had looked for

* **Newbury's boards menu is an undercount.** Fourteen on the hover menu;
  the sitemap carries Parks & Recreation, the Housing Committee and the Transfer
  Station Committee as well. Two of those three answer
  `302 → /user/login?destination=node/NN` — the site's own access control, where
  the hunt stops.
* **Five of Newbury's board links leave the town's domain.** The Energy and
  Beautification Committees run their own sites, the Fire Department a
  subdomain, the Library Trustees the library's site, and the Joint Assessing
  Board is published by the **Town of Sunapee**, because it is a joint board of
  three towns. A hunt that treats the 301 as a refusal loses five real bodies
  and is wrong about which government publishes a sixth.
* **Merrimack County's own Board of Commissioners page names no commissioner.**
  Four paragraphs and a Zoom link. All three are in the county's own annual
  report, on page 5 and again on page 6 over their signature block.
* **The county's legislative body is not its commissioners.** It is the
  DELEGATION — every state representative elected from the county, sitting
  together to vote the county budget — and this product had never named it.
* **Newbury publishes terms that expired years ago.** Cemetery Trustees at 2021,
  2022 and 2023; a Planning Board alternate at March 2021. Shipped as published,
  because correcting a term invents a fact about a named person and dropping the
  row asserts an absence the town has not.
* **The Cloudflare interstitial outgrew our size floor.** 29,809 bytes against a
  20 KB global floor, so a challenged Kearsarge page was handed to the extractor
  and reported as an empty document. The floor is now per-signature, and
  `cdn-cgi/challenge-platform` KEEPS it — Cloudflare injects that script into
  ordinary pages, and both recorded `schedulepage` fixtures carry it.

  was needed and is recorded rather than smoothed: an earlier refused `--ship`
  had copied an UNCOMMITTED `state.md` to the mirror, so the divergence check
  refused to overwrite something it could not account for — which is the check
  working. Diffed by hand, proven to be a strict PREFIX of the committed file
  (822,158 bytes against 830,698, nothing in the mirror absent from the repo),
  and only then overwritten.

## NH Hunt 2 — all forty-seven candidacies, and three walls this repo had written down (2026-08-21)

**Deployed: code `58ae918`, deploy `6a88877bf9cb300008095b2c`**, confirmed
through `/api/build` with a declared synthetic run header. A second code merge,
`fbb3006`, followed and is named as a deviation below.

### The forty-seven

Every candidate on Newbury's ballot is worked, contest by contest, local first —
Register of Probate, Register of Deeds, County Treasurer, County Attorney,
Sheriff, County Commissioner, State Representative, State Senator, Executive
Councilor, Governor, Congress, Senate. **47 of 47, in twelve contests of
twelve.** Fields owed fall **249 → 197 of 368**; FOUND rises **119 → 171**. Ten
portraits ship, every one read as an image before it did.

**`VERIFIED_ABSENT` is still 0, and that is the correct answer rather than a
missing one.** Every remaining miss has a rung still owed — rung 13, the body's
own records-request path, on all of them, and rung 9 or 11 on several. Recording
`VERIFIED_ABSENT` on any of them would be asserting an absence the ladder has
not earned, which is the one thing the transparency mandate forbids outright.

### Three standing walls fell, and two of them were ours

- **`gc.nh.gov` answers a plain fetch at 200.** `CLAUDE.md` and the New
  Hampshire ballot data both record it as refusing *"every client this project
  has, browsers included."* That was true on 2026-08-14 and had stopped being
  true; nobody re-checked, because **a written-down wall reads as a fact rather
  than as a measurement with a date on it.** Four Kelly-standard fields for four
  candidates came off that host in one pass. `NH13` routes the correction to the
  author, because only he changes `CLAUDE.md`.
- **`kearsarge.org`'s board roster reads at rung 4.** `NH01` recorded a
  Cloudflare challenge that a headless browser loads and never clears. A single
  paced `curl` gets the page at 73,695 bytes — consistent with the playbook's own
  note that this host's wall is a RATE wall. `NH01` is resolved.
- **`sos.nh.gov` falls to rung 5.** Refused host-wide since 2026-08-13 and
  worked around through the Internet Archive ever since. A different egress
  reads it, PDFs included, and `cfs.sos.nh.gov` with it.

**Rung 5 is real now.** `lib/hunt/egress.ts` walks the different-egress rung the
ladder has named since the g sessions and that nothing in this repo could reach.
It is not proxy spoofing, authenticates nothing, and carries a public URL and
nothing else. Its first version reported a 404 as a 200 — the relay answers 200
and puts the origin's status in the body — which is a wall arriving through a
wall-breaker wearing a success, and it is fixed at the reader rather than at
each caller.

### What reading the image caught

Three photographs were refused that every signal short of looking said were
portraits: a file at `/images/headshots/victor-formal.jpg` with alt text
"Victor Orlando", which is a stock photograph of a flag; a campaign's `og:image`
and `twitter:image`, both the same scanned cover of a 1978 court manual; and a
"SocialShare.jpg" that is a portrait beside a wordmark. A fourth was refused on
copyright — a filename carrying a photographer's credit — and a fifth was a
television screengrab of a courtroom, which is a screengrab, a group shot and a
broadcaster's image at once.

### Kearsarge's nine emails were in the `href`s

The district's board page publishes twelve `mailto:` links: each member's NAME
is the anchor text and their district email is the `href`. An extractor reading
table CELLS as text gets the names and drops the addresses — and what it hands
back looks exactly like a page carrying no contacts. That reading was recorded
on 2026-08-17 as *"the absences are honest, not unhunted"* and repeated on
2026-08-20. **Honest-looking and wrong, and worse than a wall**, because a wall
stays open as a work item and a recorded honest absence closes the question.
Both comments are struck in place with the correction attached.

### `HUNT05` is 18 of 18, and the ledger says so

TIGER publishes no boundary for any special district, so geometry was never
going to answer this. Three documents did: which town the ZCTA falls in (109 of
109 points in Newbury), RSA 52:1 on how a village district's territory is fixed,
and the NH Department of Revenue Administration's village-district tax table,
which lists a district even at a $0.00 rate.

**Two reach 03255 and neither is in the registry** — the Merrimack County
Conservation District, whose boundaries conform to the county by RSA 432:12, and
Lake Todd Village District, whose dead website's archived history page says it
is *"located in Bradford and Newbury"* and posts its warrant *"outside the
Newbury Town Office."* `NH14` carries the wiring.

`data/states/nh/jurisdictions/special-district-territory.json` is new and is why the ledger
moved: a district resolved by a DOCUMENT had nowhere to be recorded, so the
generated ledger went on reporting all eighteen as untried while the answer sat
in an evidence page. A district absent from that file stays UNRESOLVED, which is
the default the section exists to protect.

### The Kearsarge member towns

**107 bodies across seven towns, 17 in the registry, 90 enumerated and not
wired.** Six of the seven had no bodies at all. Also: **the district publishes
SEVEN member towns, not eight** — the standing record said eight, and Croydon
is the likely source of the extra, since it tuitions in under an anchor
agreement without being a member.

Bradford's are on **TownCloud**, a vendor family this repo had not seen, whose
`/go/<slug>` path answers 200 with an empty shell for any slug — so a
status-code probe reports every guess as a hit, and all six other member towns
"existed" on it.

### `HUNT03` — the re-walk cohort

**11 records re-walked, 5 changed status, 6 confirmed.** The changed five are
the three walls above plus Kearsarge's second board page and
`newbury.nh.gov/sitemap.xml`, recorded as a 403 and reading at 200 — which is
rung 10 for every page that town has. The six unchanged are recorded with their
shape rather than their status: an empty RSS feed at 292 bytes, a 500 from a
CivicWeb API on every rung, a portal shell served where an iCal feed was
expected, a 404 sitemap, a bare `kearsarge.org` that fails TLS negotiation on
every client, and an `nh.gov/council/` path that moved.

### `RULING 50` and `RULING 51` ship

His note on `NH09` settles the photos-first ordering: **ordering is
presentation, suppression is data loss**, and a rule against one is not a rule
against the other. The ordering ships unchanged. His note on `PE04` gives the
collection disclosure a second surface: **once in the ballot section and once on
the battlecard**, declared once in `lib/ballot/collection-note.ts` so a sentence
he has rewritten once cannot drift into two. Both verified on the live deploy,
at the DOM and read as images.

### The opened-row ledger, and the thing it caught within the hour

`docs/tracker-opened.json` makes "rows opened" a checkable claim: every id
`tracker add` assigns is written down, and the build fails if one is in neither
store. It caught this session's own double-write — the same eight rows written
twice, because `tracker:add` prints its confirmation ABOVE the views summary and
a `tail -20` hid it. The duplicates were removed and the ledger entry carries a
retraction naming what became of the ids.

### The deviation

**`fbb3006` is a second code merge and RULING 1's exception does not cover it.**
RULING 20's guard reads `git ls-files`; the ten portraits were UNTRACKED when
the suite ran and TRACKED a minute later, so the gate passed and the merge left
`main` with a failing test. The gate and the staging step were in the wrong
order and the test was right both times. `pnpm assets migrate` content-addresses
the ten; the manifest goes 940 → 948 rows.

`pnpm ladder` · `pnpm probe:site` · `pnpm nh:legislator` ·
`pnpm bodies:enumerate` · `pnpm ship:candidate`, all registered in

## NH Hunt 4 — 2026-08-21: three dark towns get 59 bodies, and a lake's village district reaches the reader who lives on it

**Code merges `980a2f6` (PR #134) and `1e07e11` (PR #135).** Deploys
`6a88d20020d90c000724dc25` and `6a88d5952bc77a00081d35de`. Two code merges: the
first is the planned one, the second is RULING 1's single exception, taken for a
live self-contradiction the walk caught — and the contradiction was one the
first merge created. Both are named below. The close-out records that follow are
separate commits, because a document cannot name the commit that contains it.

### RULING 57 is law: every twig is named

The trunk is the United States, the branches are the states, and the twig is a
township water authority. **A body is never skipped for being small.** It is
NAMED first and hunted second, and a body that cannot be reached today is a
dated measurement carrying its branches rather than a decision to leave it out.
`CLAUDE.md` **76,630 → 79,374 bytes**, rationale attached; `docs/rulings.md`
carries its entry; `pnpm verify-stamps` recovers its stamp at delta 0.

The argument in one sentence, because a stripped rule reads as guidance: the
easy bodies are already covered by somebody, and a product that reaches only
those is not smaller than it could be — it is redundant.

### Bradford, Sutton and Warner had nothing here at all

Three of Kearsarge Regional School District's seven member towns, and this
registry held **not one body** for any of them — not a committee, not the select
board. All three publish a boards index AND a live calendar. Nothing had ever
asked them.

| | bodies before | bodies now | wired live |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warner | 0 | 26 | 16 |
| Sutton | 0 | 18 | 0 |
| Bradford | 0 | 15 | 15 |
| New London | 4 | 16 | 16 |
| Wilmot | 3 | 12 | 4 |
| Newbury | 16 | 16 | 16 |
| Springfield | 8 | 8 | 0 |
| **seven towns** | **31** | **111** | **67** |

**Meetings 332 → 414.** Warner 41, Bradford 22, New London 15 → 28, Wilmot
23 → 26. At 03255 a reader now reaches **160 meetings across 42 distinct
bodies**, where this morning it was 80 across roughly 15.

**Warner's list includes the Warner Village Water District** — a separate
government with its own elected commissioners and its own budget, which is the
author's own example of a twig wearing a New Hampshire name.

**The menu is an undercount, every time, and the calendar is the better
directory.** Bradford's index lists eight boards; its calendar files sittings
for a CIP Committee, a Hazard Mitigation Committee, a Facilities Use Committee
and an Independence Day Committee besides. **Wilmot's Safety Services Facility
Committee and its Transfer Station Advisory Group appear on no town index
anywhere** and exist only in the PAST view of the town's feed.

**Sutton is named and KNOWN_UNCOVERED on purpose.** Its calendar exports 1,312
events, 47 of them upcoming, and **every single one has an empty `LOCATION`**.
Wiring them would have produced eighteen bodies whose every sitting drops, or —
worse — eighteen bodies pinned at the town office because a town office is where
boards usually meet, which is a guess about a specific sitting dressed as a fact
that a reader acts on by driving somewhere. `NH34` carries the venue hunt.

### The two districts that were resolved yesterday and still could not render

`HUNT05` resolved the **Merrimack County Conservation District** and **Lake Todd
Village District** to 03255 on 2026-08-21 and wrote them into
`data/states/nh/jurisdictions/special-district-territory.json`. Nothing but the gap ledger reads
that file. **A resolution recorded where no reader-facing surface reads it is
not a resolution a reader can see.**

The conservation district's own obstacle was worse than a missing wiring row: it
shipped with `ocdId: null` under the divisionless D28 shape, and
`lib/registry/resolve.ts`'s `bodiesAt` filters on `b.ocdId && ids.has(b.ocdId)`,
so **no point on earth could return it**. RSA 432:12 says each county "is hereby
incorporated into a conservation district" whose boundaries conform to the
county. That is a division, and it is the county's.

And a claim of ours was falsified. `lib/registry/curated-bodies.ts` carried the
settled note *"no village district's boundary reaches Newbury."* The New
Hampshire Office of Business and Economic Affairs publishes a register of all
**91 village districts** with their host municipalities, and it lists **Lake Todd
Village District twice — once under Bradford and once under NEWBURY**. The note
is deleted. Lake Todd is wired LIVE against the Town of Bradford's own calendar,
which files three of its sittings; its own site is HTTP 404 at rungs 2, 3, 4, 5
and 6, and the Internet Archive answered "Temporarily Offline" on the day.

Eleven twig rows ship in all: Lake Todd (Newbury and Bradford), the New
London–Springfield Water System Precinct (New London and Springfield, three
named commissioners meeting the first Monday at 4pm), Highland Haven, the
Ashuelot Pond Dam Precinct, Emerald Lake, Andover Village District, Andover Fire
District and East Andover Fire Precinct.

**Two official enumerations disagree and that is a finding.** The Ashuelot Pond

**Owed fields 196 → 184 of 368.** The county contests, before → after: County

Treasurer 8 → 8, Register of Probate 4 → 4. Forty-eight owed across the six

only portrait-shaped image his site publishes is a campaign photograph of him

**0 false sentences rendering**, across four zips and three surfaces each, read

### Item 7 — the jobs, and what 39% becomes nationally

| workflow | reading | cause |
|---|---|---|
| `refresh-meetings-snapshot` | 14 of 37 | **JOB, ours.** Two causes in that history; one fixed 2026-08-20, one fixed here |
| `refresh-dotgov-snapshot` | 1 of 8 | **JOB, ours, already fixed** — the one failure is the deliberate dispatch that proved the gate had no browser |
| `intake-tripwire` | 2 of 8 | **NEITHER.** Both are the ALARM FIRING, which is the job working |

The live meetings cause: `ical: fetched 3 document(s) and extracted 0
meeting(s)`, with **every drop counter at zero** — and zero drops is the tell,
because with three rows over one feed any event at all would have produced
`notConfigured` hits on the rows it did not belong to. The document carried **no
`VEVENT`**. `politeGetText` cannot catch it; NH Hunt 3 taught the fetch layer to
refuse a blank body and a wrong-format body, and this is the third shape — a
well-formed `BEGIN:VCALENDAR` envelope with nothing inside. The row is refused
now, which routes it into carry-forward instead of failing the whole source.

**What 37.8% becomes at national volume, stated plainly.** The refresh commits
only if EVERY source succeeded. Eleven sources at that whole-run rate implies
about **4.2% per source per run**. A national corpus needs a source instance per
distinct feed or portal; at 5,000 of them the chance every one succeeds in a
single run is `(1 − 0.042)^5000`, which **rounds to zero**. At a tenth of that
per-source rate it is `1.4 × 10⁻¹¹`. The gate stops being a gate and becomes a
permanent refusal to publish. What it protects is real and must survive; the
proposal is per-SOURCE failure semantics, and `NH31` puts that decision in front
of the author.

The two-consecutive detector was proved against a window whose outcome is
already known — `--asof=2026-08-20T14:00:00Z` names runs `32372995194` and
`32342602616`, names the failing step and queues the row. **I did not induce a
real failure on `main` to prove it**: breaking a governed artifact's job on
purpose is an outward-facing, hard-to-reverse act, and `--asof` exists precisely
so the proof does not need one.

### The second merge, and it fixes something the first one broke

The live walk at 03255 found the product **rendering Lake Todd Village
District's meetings while the coverage note on the same page said we had not
worked out whether it reaches this ZIP code** — with Lake Todd among the
eighteen it named. Item 4 made that sentence false, and I did not notice until I
read the capture as an image.

`stamp-coverage-tiers.mts` counted every special district in an overlapping
county as unresolved and never read the territory file. It does now: **03255
stamps 5 governments resolved against 3, and 16 unresolved against 18.**

Two defects in my own fix, both caught by asking for a count rather than an exit
code. The first loader iterated `district.reaches` unguarded, threw on the third
row — sixteen of eighteen carry no `reaches` key because their territory is
unresolved — and the surrounding `try/catch` turned the throw into an empty map;
the stamp came out byte-identical and looked like a correct no-op. It prints
what it read now. The second moved two districts into the resolved column
without moving them in the tier DISTRIBUTION, and
`tests/coverage-tier.test.ts` item 3.1 caught it in the same run.

### Class sweeps, found and fixed

- **41 committed portraits over 600 KB, largest 15 MB.** 41 found, 40 rewritten,

## NH Hunt 3 — 2026-08-21: the ladder becomes a tree, and ten recorded absences out of ten were wrong

**Code merge `2440915` (PR #133), deploy `6a88b047d0f60a0008bb2a90`.** One
planned code merge under RULING 1, eight commits. The close-out records that
follow it are separate and are labelled as such: a document cannot name the
commit that contains it.

### The headline: an absence is not a finding, and this repo had 87 of them

Ten recorded absences were re-walked under the new tree model. **Ten were
wrong.** Not one survived contact with a second branch.

87 of the 133 MISS records in `candidate-links-2026.json` came from one
generator and carried one sentence:

> no sitting officeholder in this state's registry matches this name exactly,
> **so there is no official page for us to link**

The first clause is a true fact about US. The word **so** turns it into a claim
about THEM. It was attached to Katie Hobbs, the sitting Governor of Arizona;
to Adrian Fontes, Kris Mayes, Kimberly Yee and Tom Horne, every one a sitting
Arizona statewide officer; to Andy Biggs, Juan Ciscomani and Adelita Grijalva
in Congress; and to Daniel Innis and Karen Ebel, sitting members of the New
Hampshire General Court. Every one answered a plain rung-2 fetch on the first
URL tried, and named the person.

**The join is not the defect and is unchanged** — exact normalised match within
one state, nothing fuzzy, which is the D40 discipline and correct. What was
wrong was reporting its failure as a finding about a person. Note it fails for
two quite different reasons it cannot tell apart: the person holds no office, or
they do and our registry spells them differently. Neither is evidence about
their page.

### The wall that was compiled into a skip

`scripts/audit-officials.mts` line 85 read
`if (/gc\.nh\.gov/.test(url)) return "UNVERIFIABLE-INLINE"`. **84 New Hampshire
officials were reported unverifiable on every run without a request ever being
made**, on the strength of a TLS measurement taken 2026-08-17.

A wall compiled into a skip is the worst form of what RULING 52 was adopted
over, because it cannot be disproved by the instrument that records it: the
audit could never notice the wall had fallen, having stopped asking. Removed,
and the audit re-run:

| | before 2026-08-16 | after 2026-08-21 |
|---|---|---|
| audited | 661 | 661 |
| pages fetch-verified | 577 | **655** |
| page misses | 0 | 6 |
| unverifiable inline | **84** | **0** |

78 officials recovered — and **6 genuine misses surfaced that the blanket
label had been hiding**, which is the second cost of a wall nobody re-tests.

### RULING 52 and RULING 53 are law

`CLAUDE.md` **72,082 → 76,630 bytes**, with the rationale attached including the
locked-building passage and the second half stated as inseparable from the
first. `lib/hunt/discovery.ts` is the machinery; `VERIFIED_ABSENT` now requires
**two INDEPENDENT branches**, and branches sharing a `through` collapse to one —
three fetches of one host with different headers is ONE branch walked at three
rungs, and counting it as three is how `gc.nh.gov` came to be recorded as
refusing everything.

`pnpm stale` reads every dated measurement and reports what is past its window:
**0 stale of 39** today, the oldest wiring row 8 days against a 14-day window.
It reads 39 of 39 dated rows — the 40th `verifiedAt` in `source-wiring.ts` is
the type declaration — and names its own blind spots on every run.

**Walls corrected in `CLAUDE.md`: 0, and that is reported rather than
manufactured.** The `gc.nh.gov` sentence `NH13` names went out on 2026-08-20
when Prompt C rewrote External sources. Three live false claims were corrected
elsewhere, plus the compiled skip above.

### A status is not a document

`Refresh meetings snapshot` died on `ical: fetched 3, extracted 0, drops 0` —
RULING 43 working exactly as designed, with the defect one layer up in the fetch
layer RULING 43 says in as many words it does not cover. `politeGetText`
accepted any non-challenge HTTP 200 as a document. It now refuses a blank body
for every caller and a wrong-format body for callers that declare one, on both
return paths including the curl rung.

**Class swept: 2 found outside the shared path, 2 fixed.** `congress` and
`plural` hand-roll their own backoff around a bare `fetch` and were each
accepting a blank 200 as a complete roster — every member of Congress, or a
state's whole legislature, reading as absent. Neither is on the meetings path,
so neither would ever have surfaced through the nightly refresh.

### The jobs now tell someone

Measured over the window to 2026-08-21, as pairs:

| workflow | failures of completed runs |
|---|---|
| `refresh-meetings-snapshot` | **14 of 36** |
| `intake-tripwire` | 2 of 8 |
| `refresh-dotgov-snapshot` | 1 of 8 — a third nobody had named |
| `refresh-fec-snapshot` | 0 of 1 |
| `refresh-legiscan-snapshot` | 0 of 2 |

RULING 56 ships as `lib/ops/job-watch.ts`, `scripts/watch-workflows.mts` and
`.github/workflows/job-watch.yml`, daily at 15:40 UTC after the other jobs have
had their slot. Two consecutive failures opens a Needs Sean row. It never
resolves one.

**Proved without breaking anything to prove it**: `--asof` holds the detector
against a window whose outcome is already known.
`--asof=2026-08-20T14:00:00Z` finds the meetings refresh, names runs
